label: Whiteboard
review:
- This video is a Whiteboard explainer, and the following are its intended, approved look: one large, flat, near-white board with a few very faint grey marks of old lessons; handwriting and simple line doodles in at most three marker inks (charcoal, blue, orange) and one yellow highlighter stroke per region; a floating marker with a soft shadow that writes and draws each item a moment after the narrator says it, hops from one item to the next, and leaves the frame during longer pauses; the camera resting on one region of the board, creeping in slightly, then gliding to the next region without a cut; regions written earlier showing at the edge of the frame; an ending that pulls back to the whole board with an orange circled number on each region; captions on a pale plate in the lower part of the frame. Do NOT report any of these as defects, and do not suggest adding photographs, people, characters, colour fills or texture: their absence is the style. Writing that lands about half a second after the word is intended. Small writing during the final pull-back is intended; the map is read as a whole.
- Do report: writing or a doodle overlapping other writing, text cut off at the frame edge, writing too small to read on a phone while the camera rests on a region, writing that says something different from the narration, an arrow that points at the wrong thing, a highlight or circle on a phrase the narration is not stressing, writing that arrives more than about a second after the word it shows, and a stretch of more than about three seconds where nothing new is drawn and the camera does not move.
script:
Every beat's `visual` is a **board** brief: what gets written or drawn for this step (the keyword, the number or formula, the simple object, such as a coin, a padlock or a bicycle) and how it connects to the last step. The video is one whiteboard throughout, so a role is a simple doodle or a written word, never a figure.

The narration is a teacher at a board. Work the idea out one step per sentence, in two to six steps, each building on the last: the setup, the first step, the next, the result. Say the numbers and the formula out loud as they are built ("one hundred times one point one is one hundred and ten"), since the marker writes them as you say them. Start each new step with a new sentence, because the camera moves to a fresh part of the board there. End on one closing sentence that names the whole idea in a few words: the video pulls back to show the whole board on it. A named person or place is written on the board or drawn as a simple doodle with a label. Never write a beat that needs a photograph: this style has none.

picture.opening: Region 1 is drawing from frame 0: its first item is a doodle at frame 0 that draws the first sentence's subject. Never a blank board, and never words alone.
picture.turn: A camera glide to a new region on the first word of a turn or a re-opening, or a doodle or arrow drawn in the current region at that moment.
picture.payoff: The region the answer lives in gets the biggest doodle and the region's highlight.
picture.ending: This style ends on its recap: after the payoff region the camera pulls back to the whole board at recapFrame and the region numbers pop in. Nothing after the recap.

best_for: maths and physics where a formula or a quantity is built up
money arithmetic worked out: interest, prices, percentages
a chain of causes that ends in one picture
two ideas compared side by side
a mental model, a rule of thumb or a definition
avoid_for: components passing requests, packets or data between them (System Flow draws those)
real, named things the viewer should see as pictures (Motion Graphics)
generic roles acting out a scene (Stick)
signals: the script works something out step by step
numbers or a formula are built up as the narration goes
the idea is a chain of causes that ends in one picture
one object with forces or arrows acting on it
the steps of the argument should end on one map
a definition or a rule is the point of the video
